newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombian court topples economic emergency plan.
newsitem.headline: Colombian court topples economic emergency plan.

text.p: Colombia's Constitutional Court ruled the government's economic emergency plan unconstitutional after a 6-3 vote early Wednesday evening, a court spokesman said.

The ruling overturns the economic emergency, introduced by President Ernesto Samper through a series of decrees in mid- January. The plan aimed to rein in the yawning fiscal deficit which ran at 4 percent of gross domestic product in 1996.

Alejandro Martnez, a member of the Constitutional Court, announced the ruling just minutes after the government issued a statement congratulating the lower house of Congress for approving the January 13 decree.
The Senate also approved the declaration of the state of economic emergency in a session Tuesday.

Another court member, Vladimiro Naranjo, said the court made its ruling after deciding the economic problems were not the result of abrupt and unforeseen circumstances -- the basic requirement needed to declare a state of emergency.

Measures adopted as part of the emergency, including an increase in value added tax and a six percent tax on foreign loans, would be reviewed on a case by case basis, Naranjo said. But he said that all the emergency decrees had lost the power of law as a result of the court ruling.

Samper declared the state of economic emergency on Jan. 13 came against the backdrop of a sharp economic slowdown in 1996, coupled with a steady strengthening of the country's peso currency, which undermined export activities. The fiscal deficit burgeoned to four percent of GDP in 1996 up from 0.2 percent in 1995.

The plan was aimed at shoring up tax revenues and combating evasion which was estimated at $2 billion per year. It clamped a 16 percent sales tax on a wide variety of services that were previously exempt, including insurance, reinsurance, the protection of intellectual property rights, consultancy and entertainments offered in Colombia by foreign-based companies.
Under the emergency the government also took steps to slash back its debt program and introduced a new tax on loans contracted abroad by private and public-sector companies.
Many business leaders bridled at the tax on new foreign loans arguing it would drive up import costs, put inflationary pressure on the economy and slow Colombia's economic opening.

Business leaders also argued that the surge in the value of the peso at the end of 1996 was caused more than anything else by government privatization revenues from the sale of a number of power plants and could have been avoided.
There was no immediate reaction from government circles on the court ruling, which promises to wreak havoc with economic and fiscal policy for the remainder of 1997.

Plans to slash back 1.3 trillion pesos from the national budget will not be affected by the ruling since the cuts were the subject of legislation approved by Congress before the economic emergency was declared.
In issuing the emergency decree Samper said failure to curb the fiscal deficit could result in massive public sector job cuts.
